The paper was presented at the 47th AIAA/ASME/ASCE/AHS/ASC Structures, Structural Dynamics, and Materials Conference in Newport, Rhode Island, May 1-4, 2006.

The methodology addresses a critical gap in existing probabilistic methods by incorporating inspection intervals and damage-detection capabilities, which few previous approaches had adequately addressed.
Traditional deterministic design approaches result in substantial weight and cost penalties due to their conservative assumptions about simultaneous worst-case scenarios.
The probability of failure formula uses the product of (1 - Pf(Si, ti)) terms across all intervals to calculate cumulative failure probability.
Monte Carlo simulation can compute probability of failure levels from 10^-3 to 10^-5 per life in less than 10 seconds on a typical office PC.
The number of damages per life (ND) follows a Poisson distribution, reflecting the assumption that damage events are rare and random.
The number of inspections to detect damage follows a geometric probability distribution with parameter p dependent on damage size.
The cumulative distribution function of maximum load per time is expressed as Flmax(Si, ti) = e^(-H(Si)ti), where H(Si) is the load exceedance frequency.
In the example calculation presented, the probability of encountering a failure load while the structure is compromised by damage is 1 in 4260 (4.26 × 10^-2).
The methodology considers two classes of mechanical damages: manufacturing defects (generated at t=0) and operational damages (scattered uniformly over life).
Damage types include through cracks, indentations, delaminations, and disbonding, each requiring different analysis approaches.
The probability of damage detection is a function of both damage size and type, requiring empirical data from inspection tests.
Environmental exposure effects are modeled as quasi-random strength knockdown factors that vary linearly over time rather than remaining constant.
The strength recovery coefficient is defined as the ratio of average failure load after repair to that of a new structure.
The model uses a simplified temperature description where correlation between temperature and load is hidden in different flight segments or design load cases.
For most continuous load probability density functions, linearly changing residual strength can be approximated by constant strength equal to the mean value between interval endpoints.
The methodology incorporates data from in-service experience to optimize the benefits of using composites while maintaining safety.
Composite structures are fatigue and corrosion resistant but are much more sensitive to impact damage than metal structures due to their brittle behavior.
The paper identifies that composite structures may sustain significant internal damage with no visible external evidence, making inspection and detection critical.
The methodology enables quantitative assessment of accidental, random damage events, allowing manufacturers, operators, and certification authorities to better evaluate structural safety.
The approach combines elements from the 'Level of Safety' method and the 'Probabilistic Design of Composite Structures' (ProDeCompos) method.
The NESSUS software package, developed by Southwest Research Institute, is used to obtain probabilistic characteristics of initial and residual strength.
The simulation flowchart includes steps for generating initial strength, damage initiation, damage size, number of inspections, repair, and residual strength assessment.
The load exceedance curve parameters used in the example are H0 = 4.2683 × 10^9 and b = 0.112742.
The methodology can handle multiple design load cases, damage types, and inspection types simultaneously, making it applicable to complex aircraft structures.
